modes.label: νₛ(OCO)
modes.note: Both C=O bonds stretch in phase while C stays put — the totally symmetric stretch, conventionally ν₁. Centrosymmetric, so by the mutual exclusion rule it's IR-inactive but Raman-active.

modes.label: νₐₛ(OCO)
modes.note: One C=O bond lengthens as the other shortens, in antiphase — the asymmetric stretch, conventionally ν₃. Breaks the molecule's center of symmetry, making it IR-active (and, by the mutual exclusion rule, Raman-inactive).

modes.label: δ(OCO)
modes.note: Both O's swing the same way in-plane while C recoils oppositely, closing and opening the O-C-O angle — the in-plane component of the doubly-degenerate bend, conventionally ν₂. Degenerate with the out-of-plane wagging component below; together the pair is why ν₂ is IR-active.

modes.label: ω(OCO)
modes.note: The same ν₂ bending motion as above, but out of the molecular plane — shown here as the atoms pulsing in size rather than a real 2D displacement, since a flat diagram can't otherwise depict out-of-plane motion. Frequency-coincident with the in-plane scissoring component, so it has no separately resolved band of its own.

modes.label: ν(CO)
modes.note: C and O move apart and together along the single bond — the only vibration a two-atom molecule can have, so there's no symmetric/asymmetric pair and nothing to number ν₁/ν₂/ν₃-style.

modes.label: ν(CH)
modes.note: The C-H bond stretches — the key HCOO* marker band, since no other common surface species shares this exact C-H environment. In Fermi resonance with the δ(OCH)+νₐₛ(OCO) combination band on some supports (e.g. CeO₂), splitting into a doublet. The free formate ion has its own conventional ν-numbering in the vibrational-spectroscopy literature (this mode is commonly cited as ν₁), though the exact assignment order varies by source more than CO₂'s does.

modes.label: νₐₛ(OCO)
modes.note: One C-O bond lengthens as the other shortens, in antiphase — often cited as ν₄ of the free formate ion. Independent of surface binding topology: position is support-dependent, so both monodentate and bidentate coordination are listed below.

modes.label: νₛ(OCO)
modes.note: Both C-O bonds stretch in phase — often cited as ν₂ of the free formate ion. Paired with νₐₛ(OCO) above; the splitting between the two (Δν) is itself diagnostic of binding geometry. Independent of surface binding topology, so both monodentate and bidentate coordination are listed below.

modes.label: δ(OCH)
modes.note: The C-H bond rocks relative to the O-C-O frame, changing the O-C-H angle — often cited as ν₃ of the free formate ion. Often overlaps νₛ(OCO) and isn't always separately resolved in a spectrum.

modes.label: νₐₛ(OCO)
modes.note: Two of the three C-O bonds stretch oppositely (one lengthens, one shortens) while the third stays put — one component of the doubly-degenerate asymmetric stretch, ν₃ of the free CO₃²⁻ ion (D₃h symmetry); surface binding splits that degenerate pair into two resolved frequencies. For monodentate carbonate on CaO, Solis et al. (Fig. 5) assign the higher-frequency resolved component as their ν₆ (asymmetric stretch ν(C-O)), 1450–1490 cm⁻¹ — close to this mode's own monodentate band (1480–1520 cm⁻¹). Independent of surface binding topology — listed for both monodentate (smaller splitting from νₛ) and bidentate (larger splitting) coordination, since the splitting itself is diagnostic of which one it is.

modes.label: νₛ(OCO)
modes.note: The two non-surface-bound C-O bonds stretch in phase — the other resolved component of the same doubly-degenerate ν₃ pair (paired with νₐₛ(OCO) above), not the free ion's true totally-symmetric stretch ν₁ (which stays IR-inactive and isn't separately resolved here). For monodentate carbonate on CaO, Solis et al. (Fig. 5) assign this lower-frequency component as their ν₅ (symmetric stretch ν(C-O)+ν(C-Os), where Os is the surface oxygen), 1350–1370 cm⁻¹ — close to this mode's own monodentate band (1380–1420 cm⁻¹). Independent of surface binding topology — listed for both monodentate and bidentate coordination.

modes.label: δ(OCO)
modes.note: Two of the three O's swing toward/apart in-plane while the third stays fixed — one component of the doubly-degenerate in-plane bend, ν₄ of the free ion, again resolved into two frequencies by surface binding. For monodentate carbonate on CaO, Solis et al. (Fig. 5) assign this resolved component as their ν₁ (asymmetric bending δ(OsCO), Os = surface oxygen), 680–700 cm⁻¹ — close to this band's own 650–715 cm⁻¹ range. Generic surface carbonate, not specific to a binding mode; the bidentate case isn't separately diagrammed in that source, but is assumed analogous.

modes.label: γ(OCO)
modes.note: The central C moves out of the O-C-O plane while the O's stay put — the out-of-plane bend, ν₂ of the free ion, non-degenerate so it doesn't split on binding. For monodentate carbonate on CaO, Solis et al. (Fig. 5) assign this as their ν₃ (out-of-plane deformation π), 850–860 cm⁻¹ — close to this band's own 860–890 cm⁻¹ range.
